reels.title: The cloud in one sentence
reels.body: The cloud means renting someone else's computers over the internet. No hardware to buy: pay for what you use and scale anytime.

reels.title: Meet Amazon S3
reels.body: S3 (Simple Storage Service) is object storage in the cloud: upload files of any type and reach them from anywhere with an internet connection.

reels.title: Buckets, objects and keys
reels.body: Files are objects stored in buckets. Each object has a key (its name), like photos/cat.jpg. Reach them via console, CLI or code.

flashcards.front: How much data can S3 hold?
flashcards.back: Virtually unlimited. No disks to add or capacity to plan; your storage simply grows as you upload.
It's designed for 99.999999999% (11 nines) durability, so losing a stored object is extremely unlikely.

quiz.q: What kind of storage is Amazon S3?
quiz.why: S3 stores files as objects in buckets. Databases and virtual machines are separate AWS services.

quiz.q: In S3, what is a file called?
quiz.why: Files are objects; buckets are the containers that hold them.

quiz.q: S3 is designed for 11 nines of what?
quiz.why: 99.999999999% durability means stored data is extremely unlikely to be lost.

quiz.q: Who can see a brand-new bucket's contents?
quiz.why: New buckets are private by default, with Block Public Access on.

quiz.q: Which job is NOT a typical S3 use case?
quiz.why: Running code is a compute job, perfect for Lambda. S3 stores data.
